keyVerseText: And Salmon begat Booz of Rachab; and Booz begat Obed of Ruth; and Obed begat Jesse;
rootMeaning: The Greek word Ἰεσσαί (Iessaí) is of Hebrew origin, derived from יִשַׁי (Yishay), which means 'I possess.' This root meaning conveys a sense of possession or ownership, which enriches the common English name 'Jesse' beyond a mere personal identifier. Jesse is known biblically as the father of King David, anchoring the name in the lineage of Israel's monarchy and God's covenantal promises.
usageInScripture: The term Ἰεσσαί appears five times in the New Testament, consistently translated as 'Jesse' or referring to someone 'of Jesse' or 'the son of Jesse.' This uniformity in translation underscores its role as a proper noun identifying a key patriarchal figure. The references in Matthew, Luke, Acts, and Romans connect Jesse to the genealogy and messianic fulfillment through David, highlighting the name's significance in tracing Jesus' royal lineage.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding Ἰεσσαί as 'I possess' deepens our appreciation of God's sovereign ownership in the unfolding of redemptive history. Jesse, as the father of David, represents the human link in God's covenantal plan to bring forth the Messiah. Recognizing Jesse's place in Scripture reminds believers that God's promises are fulfilled through ordinary people within a divinely orchestrated genealogy. This word anchors the Christian faith in the historical reality of Jesus' Davidic lineage, affirming His rightful kingship and messianic identity.
keyVerseReflection: Matthew 1:5 traces the genealogy leading to Jesse, stating, 'And Salmon begat Booz of Rachab; and Booz begat Obed of Ruth; and Obed begat Jesse.' The inclusion of Jesse here highlights his pivotal role as the father of David, connecting Jesus to this royal line. The word Ἰεσσαί in this verse emphasizes the continuity of God's covenant through generations, reassuring believers of the faithfulness of God's redemptive plan culminating in Christ.
